item.title: The case of 38 tokens per second: why the M3 Ultra started with twelve
item.description:
It all started with a seemingly simple task.

I wanted to use Qwen3.8-27B locally in BF16. Not the original PyTorch checkpoint through some random compatibility layer, but mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-bf16 — a specially prepared MLX format version for Apple Silicon. The entire Qwen3.8 series from mlx-community is converted specifically for running on Apple processors.

That is, the model was already adapted for the Mac architecture. No 8-bit or 4-bit quantization, because the original priority was not to get a nice benchmark number at any cost. I needed maximum model accuracy for complex analysis, code work, and long reasoning.

It seemed like there would be no hardware issues at all.

My configuration is a 2025 Mac Studio (Mac15,14, custom order number Z1CE001BMZP/A) with Apple M3 Ultra: 32 CPU cores, 24 of which are performance cores, 80 GPU cores, 512 GB of unified memory, and a 2 TB SSD. Apple's stated memory bandwidth is 819 GB/s.

So this is not a laptop that accidentally got tasked with running a large language model. This is the maximum configuration of the M3 Ultra in terms of CPU, GPU, and memory capacity.

And on this machine, the optimized for Apple Silicon version of Qwen3.8-27B in BF16 was producing only 12 tokens per second.

At first, the result seemed suspicious. The machine has dozens of CPU and GPU cores, the model fits entirely in memory, and the native Apple Silicon framework MLX is used. So why is the speed nowhere near what you'd expect from a top-tier GPU?

I started looking for the bottleneck.

Read more

item.title: A mirror for people. How I made a readable version of a forum where only AI agents communicate.
item.description:

But then a feeling of injustice started gnawing at me — and in the end I built a window for humans for it — 1f916.xrayfun.ru. I'll tell you why, how, and what came of it.

item.title: Marketing analysis of the market and competitors with AI in one day instead of a month
item.description:
Good marketing analysis is the foundation of almost any new project. Until you understand who your audience is, who your competitors are, what their offers and prices are, there is simply nowhere to go. Previously, such analysis took two to three weeks, and sometimes a whole month of manual work. Now this process can be accelerated many times over thanks to neural networks. 

Hi! My name is Dmitry Satarov, I am the head of the agency "Hey, Startup!" and a course mentor at "Neural Networks for Marketing" at Yandex Practicum. When decent neural networks appeared in 2022–2023, I started building a process that would allow marketing research to be performed significantly faster. I'll share it in this article.

item.title: Pre-IPO of foreign IT and AI companies: explaining how the market works.
item.description:
Early investors in Anthropic, SpaceX, or OpenAI earned multiples, but not by buying shares on IPO day. The main growth occurred earlier, during the private financing stage, when these companies were not yet available to the broad market.

This stage is called Pre-IPO — the last major round before going public. The article breaks down how the foreign Pre-IPO market for IT and AI companies works, what its potential sources of returns are, and why the legal details of a deal matter no less than the well-known brands.

Learn more

item.title: Virtual Employees Instead of AI Assistants: How Agents Learn to Work Inside a Company
item.description:
Development is gradually changing the traditional division of labor between humans and tools. AI is taking over not individual operations, but sequences of actions that previously required a specialist's involvement. However, as autonomy grows, the requirements for the system itself are also changing. An agent must understand the project context, know internal rules, and have access to the tools the team uses—not just search for information and write code.

This topic was discussed in detail at the eighth MWS meetup for DevOps and SRE. Experts from MTC Web Services and Orion Soft highlighted different aspects of the transition to agent-based development and shared cases of how AI is gradually turning into a virtual employee—an agent that operates without constant human supervision—and what needs to change in engineering processes to achieve this.

item.title: End of fat margins for AI: all about pricing and low model costs
item.description:
Recently, the AI field has not just been declining, but is even entering an active stage of competition between several fronts — corporate AI (OpenAI and Anthropic, which are also competing with each other) versus open models (Qwen, GLM, DeepSeek).

Token prices sometimes drop, and when they cannot reduce the price, they create lightweight models with low cost. Reducing inference cost is no longer just a side effect of optimization but has become the main axis of competition. OpenAI's decision to lower prices on GPT 5.6 Sol at least until November 2026 is an attempt to regain its market share through dumping. Open models are no longer catching up to closed ones in quality, but sometimes even surpass them in usage economics, making AI access a utility service.

In this article, we will analyze the impact of Qwen, GLM, and other open-source models, the competition in the AI market, and finally examine where the AI race has turned this time.

item.title: Ox Alpha (GLM-5.3-Flash). What was that?
item.description:
On August 20, the line stealth/ox-alpha appeared on OpenRouter. No model card, not even a hint as to who released it. The provider was listed as "Anonymous." The price – zero. The context – a million. The platform warned: we are not the owner of this model, we just route the requests.

Six days later, the anonymous entity had a name, tens of trillions of processed tokens, and half a million developers who had already dumped working code into it in the meantime. Spoiler that is no longer a spoiler: it turned out to be GLM-5.3-Flash from China's Z.ai.

But the journey from "something unclear" to "frontier model" turned out to be dramatic and deserves a breakdown. And since I personally stared at this thread for almost a week, refreshing the feed like a man possessed – let me tell you what happened there, step by step.

Read more

item.title: From Copilot to AI Factory: where AI is already paying off and what should a developer focus on?
item.description:
Sometimes it happens that a company purchases artificial intelligence before it has time to understand what it needs it for — and yes, this is a tribute to chaos and the fear of falling behind in the race. The CEO has already heard at a forum that agents will replace half the office; the innovation director has already promised a pilot by the end of the quarter; HR has ordered a webinar on prompts for employees, because any technological change in Russia first and foremost requires a webinar; and the CFO sits in a meeting, flipping through a presentation, trying to find the slide where all this new digital life finally turns into money. Only that slide isn't there yet. But by lunchtime, the neural network has written a congratulatory message to the CEO, and by evening, an order has appeared to create a working group — the implementation, one might say, has been a success, everyone is pleased.

I am deliberately exaggerating, but only slightly (I expressed myself very cautiously). Artificial intelligence is already delivering quite tangible benefits to business: it reduces the time for processing inquiries, brings newcomers up to the level of more experienced employees, manages inventory, detects defects, predicts breakdowns, and processes documents faster than people who, just yesterday, had to transfer data from one window to another while maintaining the expression of someone engaged in intellectual labor. However, money appears not where the model better simulates a conversation partner, but where it is embedded in a repetitive operation and is accountable to a metric that is not impressed by the quality of a demo or the number of parameters: time, cost, error rate, downtime, turnover, or profit.

Read more

item.title: Yet Another English - and yes, another site for learning English, well what can you do?
item.description:
Well, as you might have guessed, I named the service that way to immediately address the main objection (hehe). Yes, I know there are thousands of them — and I made another one, and I'll explain why below.

I have weak English, about B1 (but for product management, you usually need a higher level, you know). I watch YouTube in English to improve it and constantly come across unfamiliar words. Writing them down in a table, loading them into Anki — I was too lazy. I wanted it like this: throw a link to a video — words of my level would automatically be extracted from the subtitles and placed in a queue for repetition.

I work a lot, usually have 1–2 hours in the evenings. So over a couple of months of such evenings (595 commits) I got a trainer: a PWA in React, data lives in the user's IndexedDB, plus a dictionary and various exercises.

From an "AI-era website" you expect that inside it's a wrapper over a chatbot, RAG, and all that stuff, you know. Mine turned out the opposite: the LLM here is a contractor for two narrow tasks, while the main work is done by frequency lists, an algorithm from the 90s, and Claude as a workhorse. That's what this article, or series of articles, will be about.

Read more
